name: Teushen
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Para el teushen y el haush, las fuentes presentan en general pocos datos sobre el acento, pero no dicen nada sobre la posible existencia de tono en estas lenguas. [p. 150] ... 5.1.3. Indicios sobre el acento en teushen. En Malaspina (códice 17603, Outes 1913: 447) se menciona la “…necesidad de recargar el acento, y aun hacer una leve pausa sobre una sola silaba, pronunciando luego rapidamente las demas silabas hasta concluir las palabras”, lo que sugiere que en teushen había un acento de intensidad fijo en la sílaba inicial de las palabras. [p. 152]
new_statements.translation: For Teushen and Haush the sources in general present few data on accent, but say nothing about the possible existence of tone in these languages. [p. 150] ... 5.1.3. Indications about accent in Teushen. In Malaspina (codex 17603, Outes 1913: 447) mention is made of the '...need to load the accent, and even to make a slight pause, on a single syllable, then pronouncing the remaining syllables rapidly until the words are finished', which suggests that in Teushen there was a fixed intensity (stress) accent on the initial syllable of words. [p. 152]
new_statements.citation: Viegas Barros, J. Pedro. 2015. Proto-Chon: fonología, morfología y léxico. Tesis doctoral, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Facultad de Filosofía y Letras. Vol. 1, ch. 5 'Fenómenos suprasegmentales', sec. 5.1.3 'Indicios sobre el acento en teushen'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (intensity accent) is inferred to have been fixed on the first syllable of the word; the only evidence is an 18th-century observer's (Malaspina expedition, 1789) remark that one syllable is emphasised and paused on and the rest of the word run through quickly. Viegas Barros presents this as a suggestion ('sugiere'), consistent with his reconstruction of proto-Chon stress on the first syllable of the (main) root (sec. 5.1.4, pp. 152-153).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Teushen (secondary stress is discussed only for Selknam and Tehuelche).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Teushen. In the comparison (5.1.4) he notes Selknam/Tehuelche exceptions (e.g. non-singular pronouns) and says the original proto-Chon situation may have been different in a way that cannot yet be reconstructed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('palabras'); inference from a traveler's remark about pronunciation, not from systematically accented data. The Malaspina vocabularies are 1789 Puerto Deseado lists with mixed Southern/Northern Teushen traits. No tone is reported. No primary phonological description of Teushen exists; this is the only explicit stress statement found for the language.
new_statements.identity_note: Teushen (teus1236) is extinct and known only from wordlists (Viedma 1780 San Julián; Malaspina expedition 1789 Puerto Deseado, codices 17631a-e/17603; Elizalde 1791; d'Orbigny 1829 Carmen de Patagones; Ameghino c.1900 in Lehmann-Nitsche 1913; Molina 1967). Viegas Barros 2015 sec. 1.4.2 (p. 36) distinguishes a Southern dialect (Ameghino, Viedma) and a Northern one (d'Orbigny), and says the Malaspina-Pineda and Elizalde lists 'parecen tener rasgos mezclados de las dos presuntas variedades'. The only stress evidence comes from the Malaspina 1789 material, i.e. an unlocalised (mixed) Teushen variety; Viegas Barros 2017 also raised whether some early 'Patagón' lists (Pigafetta) are Teushen, Tehuelche or a third Chon language, but the thesis lists the Malaspina vocabularies under Teushen (sec. 1.4.1.1 item 2, pp. 34-35).
